'''Maxim Nikolaevich Chernodub'''<ref>[http://www.lattice.itep.ru/people/?name=Chernodub Chernodub Maxim Nikolaevich] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120324055255/http://www.lattice.itep.ru/people/?name=Chernodub |date=2012-03-24 }}. [[Institute for Theoretical and Experimental Physics|''Itep'']] ''Lattice'', 1998-2011, retrieved May 16, 2011</ref> (born June&nbsp;7, 1973) is a French [[physicist]] of Ukrainian descent best known for his postulation of the magnetic-field-induced [[superconductivity]] of the [[vacuum]].

== Career ==
=== Beginnings and degrees ===

Chernodub attended Lycée 145 in [[Kyiv]] from 1980 to 1990. He earned a bachelor's degree and a Master of Science, at the [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]], in 1993 and 1996, respectively, and a Ph.D. at the [[Institute for Theoretical and Experimental Physics]] (ITEP) in Moscow, in 1999. In 2007, there followed his habilitation at the ITEP.<ref name=cv>[http://www.lmpt.univ-tours.fr/~maxim/Files/maxim_chernodub_cv_short.pdf Curriculum Vitae of Maxim Chernodub] (May 2011; PDF file)</ref>

=== Work as a scientist ===

Chernodub worked for the ITEP (1994–2001, 2003–2006, 2007–2008) and for the Japanese [[Kanazawa University|Kanazawa]] (2001–2003) and [[Hiroshima University]] (2006–2007). Since 2008, he holds a permanent position as a researcher for the [[French National Centre for Scientific Research]] (CNRS), at the [[:fr:Laboratoire de mathématiques et physique théorique|Laboratoire de mathématiques et physique théorique]] of the [[François Rabelais University|University of Tours]].<ref name=cv /> He is also a visiting professor at the Department of Physics and Astronomy, [[Ghent University]] ([[Belgium]]; 2010–2012),<ref name=cv /> and a referee for the [[Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council|Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada]], the Russian [[Ministry of Education and Science (Russia)|Ministry of Education and Science]], and the French [[Agence Nationale de la Recherche|National Agency for Research]].<ref name=cv />

== The magnetic-field-induced superconductivity of the vacuum ==

Chernodub found, on the basis of the theory of [[quantum chromodynamics]] (QCD), that charged [[rho meson]]s<ref name=McKee /> — [[Charged particle|charged]] [[virtual particle]]s popping into and out of being in a vacuum — can linger long enough to become real in a [[magnetic field]] of 10<sup>16</sup>&nbsp;tesla or more.<ref name=McKee>[https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg21028073.800-how-to-turn-the-vacuum-into-a-superconductor.html How to turn the vacuum into a superconductor]. ''[[New Scientist]]'', April 8, 2011, retrieved May 13, 2011</ref> They share the same [[quantum state]] and form a [[Vacuum expectation value|condensate]], flowing together as one particle. The condensed rho mesons may carry [[electric current]] without resistance along the magnetic field lines.<ref name=McKee /> The internal magnetic fields of the particles align with the magnetic field around them, which causes a decrease of the total energy.<ref name=McKee />

Among several unusual properties of this postulated superconductivity of the vacuum is that it would, unlike previously known superconductivity, be expected to persist at temperatures of at least a billion,<ref name=Wilkins>Alasdair Wilkins: [http://io9.com/5787141/ultra+hot-superconductors-could-spontaneously-form-in-the-vacuum-of-space Ultra-hot superconductors could spontaneously form in the vacuum of space]. ''[[io9]]'', March 30, 2011, retrieved May 13, 2011</ref> perhaps billions of degrees.<ref name=Cartwright>Jon Cartwright: [http://physicsworld.com/cws/article/news/45558 Superconductivity from nowhere]. ''Physicworld.com'', March 29, 2011, retrieved May 13, 2011</ref> Chernodub sees a possible explanation of his results in the [[quark]]s and antiquarks constituting the rho mesons being forced to move only along the magnetic field lines, which would render the rho mesons far more stable.<ref name=Cartwright /> The [[Effective mass (spring-mass system)|effective mass]] of the rho mesons would be lowered to zero, enabling them to condense and move freely, due to an interaction of their [[Spin (physics)|spin]]s with the external magnetic field.<ref name=Cartwright /> The apparently strange situation that a current should flow without a [[Charge carrier|carrier]] is explained by the fact that a vacuum is never truly empty.<ref name=Cartwright /><ref>[http://www.sciencecontrol.com/superconductivity-from-nowhere.html Superconductivity from nowhere]. ''Sciencecontrol.com'', 2011, retrieved May 13, 2011</ref>

In the realm of astrophysics, Chernodub's calculations could mean that periods of vacuum-superconductivity in the early days of the universe had caused the emergence of the large-scale magnetic fields out in space, which are so far mysterious.<ref name=Wilkins /><ref name=Cartwright /> At present, magnetic fields of 10<sup>16</sup>&nbsp;T are by far not reached in the known universe.<ref name=Cartwright />

=== Possible measurability at ion colliders ===

Chernodub believes that his prediction could be proven at the [[Large Hadron Collider]] (LHC) near Geneva or at the [[Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider]] (RHIC) of [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] in Upton, New York. [[Ion]]s colliding at these [[particle accelerator]]s could create a magnetic field of almost the required strength in a "near miss", for perhaps one yoctosecond. Chernodub expects that vacuum superconductivity would, if it exists, leave a trace of charged rho mesons at the accelerators.<ref name=Cartwright />
